one_liner: C HTTP/1.1 server and embeddable library; topped TechEmpower Round 10 JSON at ~5.8x Go net/http's throughput.
what_it_does: Lwan is a standalone web server driven by a `key = value` config file (static files, Lua handlers and Lua Server Pages, rewrite, redirect, FastCGI, basic auth), and also liblwan, a static/shared C library in which you declare handlers with `LWAN_HANDLER_ROUTE(name, "/route")` that fill a response buffer and return an HTTP status, then call `lwan_init` / `lwan_main_loop`. It is not a drop-in for Go net/http: handlers are C or Lua, not `http.Handler`, and the protocol is HTTP/1.x only (the HTTP/2 issue has been open since 2014). Chunked responses, server-sent events, WebSockets, and awaiting other file descriptors from inside a handler are supported.
how_it_is_fast: One worker thread per online CPU, pinned using the sysfs thread_siblings topology, each with its own SO_REUSEPORT listening socket (with a CBPF steering filter where available) and its own edge-triggered epoll set; connection state lives in one preallocated array indexed by file descriptor. Every connection runs in a stackful coroutine switched by a hand-written x86-64/aarch64 swapcontext that skips floating-point registers and the signal mask, so handlers read like blocking code with no per-request thread or callback chain. The request parser dispatches on methods and headers by loading 2/4/8 bytes as integers (`STRING_SWITCH`), finds line ends with memchr/memmem, and decodes URLs with SSE/SWAR; idle keep-alive connections expire through a timeout queue driven by a timer wheel. Release builds add LTO and `-march=native`.
when_to_use: Small, CPU-cheap HTTP/1.1 responses (JSON, plaintext, cached small files) at high connection counts, where per-request server overhead dominates; in Round 10 its lead over Go net/http grew from 1.7x at 8 connections to 5.8x at 256.
Linux x86-64 or aarch64 hosts where you build from source for the target CPU and want one pinned worker per core.
Embedding an HTTP endpoint in a C program via liblwan without a C++ runtime or an external event library.
Config-only static file or Lua serving: files under 16 KiB are mmap-cached with precompressed deflate/gzip/Brotli/zstd variants, and larger files go out via sendfile.
A fast backend stub or load target for benchmarking proxies and gateways (the README lists Kong, KrakenD and Istio using it this way).
when_not_to_use: You need HTTP/2 or HTTP/3: Lwan is HTTP/1.x only (issue #17, open since 2014).
You need production TLS: TLS is marked experimental, works only on Linux through kTLS (tls.ko plus mbedTLS), and supports TLSv1.2 only; the README suggests a separate terminator such as Hitch.

Uploads without Content-Length or of large size: a request body with no Content-Length gets 400 (no chunked request bodies), POST/PUT bodies are capped at 40,960 bytes by default, and issue #218 (open) reports pipelined requests over 4 KB failing.

An internet-facing edge that needs a hardened parser: September 2026 reports fixed request desynchronization via stale pipelined state (#381, #382), a WebSocket-FIN busy-spin that pinned a worker (#383), and an 8-byte out-of-bounds read in the SWAR URL decoder (#380); lost/stuck socket reports #348 and #353 remain open.
Proprietary software that ships the binary: Lwan is GPL-2.0-or-later, so distributing a program linked with liblwan carries GPL obligations (the README notes that only serving over HTTP does not).

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (liblwan-static / liblwan.so with installed headers), or the standalone `lwan` server binary
integration.dependencies: Required: CMake 3.20+ (CMakeLists.txt; the README still says 2.8) and one of zlib, zlib-ng or libdeflate. Optional: Lua 5.4, Brotli, zstd, mbedTLS (kTLS), mimalloc/jemalloc/tcmalloc, SQLite and MariaDB client (samples only); libucontext on architectures other than x86-64/aarch64.
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler that accepts -std=gnu11 (GCC or Clang; uses GNU extensions, inline assembly and linker sections)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 is primary (CI build, tests, static analysis, OSS-Fuzz); FreeBSD and OpenBSD x86-64 build (epoll emulated on kqueue); aarch64 has a native context switch; other CPUs fall back to libucontext, which fails on Apple Silicon macOS (issue #366). Windows not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Fixed pool of worker threads (default one per online CPU); each connection's coroutine stays on one thread, so a handler runs single-threaded per request. A handler that blocks stalls every connection on that worker; use lwan_request_await_read/write or lwan_request_sleep to yield. Shared caches use locks (issue #53). Otherwise not documented.

gotchas: The default CMake build type is Debug, which logs every request while holding a lock; benchmark only with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release.
Release builds default to -march=native/-mtune=native (MTUNE_NATIVE=ON), so a binary can fail on other CPUs; pass -DMTUNE_NATIVE=OFF when packaging.

Coroutine stacks are fixed-size (4x SIGSTKSZ, 8x with Brotli, page-rounded) and in release builds come from the heap with no guard page, so deep recursion or large stack buffers in handlers can silently overflow (see issue #130).

At startup Lwan raises RLIMIT_NOFILE and preallocates max_file_descriptors (default 524288) x sizeof(struct lwan_connection); max_file_descriptors must be at least 10x threads. A crash when threads < online CPUs was fixed only on 2026-09-18.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Lwan over Drogon, Crow, Oat++, CWIST or Agoo-C when you want a pure-C HTTP/1.1 server with the widest measured margin over Go net/http (5.8x in TFB JSON versus ~1.5x for Crow in the catalog), and GPL plus no HTTP/2 is acceptable. If you need HTTP/2 or production TLS, Lwan is the wrong choice; look at H2O or a C++ framework instead.
verified_claims_summary: TechEmpower Round 10 (April 2015), Peak Hosting dual-Xeon E5 v2 servers (40 hyperthreads) over 10 GbE, JSON-serialization test: Lwan rev 49607add (CMake Release, compiler not stated) peaked at 2,200,066 req/s at 256 connections, #1 of 145, versus 379,662 req/s for TFB's Go 1.4.2 net/http + encoding/json entry (5.8x); the ratio was 1.7x at 8 connections. In the same round's plaintext test the gap was ~2.6x (2,075,046 vs 799,052 req/s, Lwan #7, far behind ULib's 6.9M), and Lwan's JSON handler then built a ccan/json DOM per request, so the win comes from the server core, not from JSON encoding.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-22; latest tag v0.7, June 2025; September 2026 security reports were fixed within days), GPL-2.0-or-later, built from source with CMake or pulled as GHCR container images and Alpine/Arch/NixOS packages.
